nameStory: The bufflehead mason bee gets its name from its distinctively large, rounded head that resembles the puffy head of a bufflehead duck. Just like the duck's oversized noggin stands out on the water, this bee's prominent cranium makes it easily recognizable among its mason bee cousins.
description: The bufflehead mason bee is a solitary, hardworking pollinator that belongs to the mason bee family. These bees are excellent pollinators that don't live in hives like honeybees, but instead work alone to build individual nests. They're medium-sized bees with notably large heads and robust bodies. Like other mason bees, they're gentle creatures that rarely sting and are incredibly efficient at pollinating flowers.

idTips.label: Oversized Head
idTips.description: The head appears disproportionately large compared to the body, giving it a distinctive bulbous appearance that feels almost cartoonish when you get a close look

idTips.label: Dark Body Color
idTips.description: The body typically appears dark brown to black with a somewhat metallic sheen that catches the light as they move from flower to flower

idTips.label: Solitary Behavior
idTips.description: Unlike honeybees, you'll see these working alone rather than in groups, methodically visiting flowers with a businesslike efficiency

idTips.label: Fuzzy Appearance
idTips.description: The body has a distinctly hairy, almost fuzzy texture that helps them collect pollen as they brush against flower parts

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: They fly with a steady, purposeful buzz that's less frantic than honeybees, often hovering briefly before landing on flowers

habitat: Bufflehead mason bees can be found throughout New England's diverse landscapes, from suburban gardens to woodland edges and meadows. They prefer areas with abundant flowering plants and nearby nesting sites like hollow stems, wood cavities, or even artificial bee houses. Look for them in gardens, parks, orchards, and natural areas where spring and summer wildflowers are plentiful.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity time when adults emerge and begin foraging on early flowers like fruit tree blossoms and spring wildflowers. This is the best time to spot their distinctive large heads as they work methodically through gardens.
seasonality.summer: Active through early to mid-summer, continuing to forage and provision their nests. You'll see them visiting a wide variety of blooming plants during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down significantly, though some late individuals may still be seen. Most have completed their life cycle and the next generation is developing in sealed nest chambers.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; the next generation overwinters as developing larvae or pupae in their sealed nest chambers, waiting for spring's warmth to emerge.

funFact: Mason bees are so efficient at pollination that just 300 female mason bees can do the pollination work of 30,000 honeybees - they're like the Formula One race cars of the pollinator world!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other mason bees in the Osmia genus, but the bufflehead's distinctively oversized head is your best clue. Remember: if the head looks comically large compared to the body, you've likely found your bufflehead mason bee. Other mason bees have more proportionate head-to-body ratios.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their common name including 'mason bee,' these insects don't actually work with masonry or stone. They're called mason bees because they use mud, clay, or chewed plant material to build walls in their nest chambers, much like a mason builds with mortar.
compareHints: Among New England's mason bees, the bufflehead stands out primarily due to its enlarged head structure. The Blue Orchard Bee has a more metallic blue-green sheen and proportionate head, while the Horn-faced Mason Bee has distinctive horn-like projections on males. The Maine Blueberry Bee is typically smaller overall and more specialized in its flower preferences.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mason bees, the Horn-faced Mason Bee is the only one with facial horns, making identification straightforward.

Among New England's mason bees, the Blue Orchard Bee is distinguished by its intense metallic blue coloration - most other Osmia species are darker black, brownish, or have less pronounced metallic sheens.
Among New England's mason bees, the Taurus Mason Bee can be distinguished from the more common Blue Orchard Bee by its darker coloration and lack of metallic blue-green sheen.
